title: The Woman From West Bengal Whose Abdomen Would Not Stop Swelling

sections.heading: The Patient's Story
sections.content:
She is 45 years old, from West Bengal, and came to the hospital with two years of abdominal distension and two months of swelling in both feet. She had been well until two years ago, when her abdomen began to swell — gradually at first, but rapidly worsening over the last year. As her belly grew, she developed breathlessness, difficulty eating and drinking, and severe low back pain. She describes wanting to eat a variety of foods but being physically unable to. Interestingly, whenever fluid was drained from her abdomen (paracentesis), her urine output improved, her breathlessness eased, and her appetite came back — only for the distension to return.

Her feet have been swelling for two months, worse in the mornings. She has had diabetes for a year, took medication for six months, then stopped. She has no known history of high blood pressure, tuberculosis, thyroid disease, or heart disease, and no significant family history. She has seven children (four sons, three daughters) and reached menopause four and a half years ago. Her bowel movements are irregular, her sleep is inadequate, and she has no addictions or known drug allergies.

sections.heading: What the Work-Up Showed So Far
sections.content:
- **General appearance:** malnourished; clubbing present; terry nails present; possible localized lymphadenopathy around the umbilicus; no pallor, icterus, cyanosis, koilonychia, or palmar erythema
- **Vitals:** temperature 98.5°F, BP 110/90 mmHg, pulse 64 bpm (regular), RR 24/min
- **Abdominal exam:** ovoid distension with a slit-like umbilicus, no surgical scars or sinuses, engorged abdominal veins; on palpation, possible lymph nodes around the umbilicus — multiple, smooth, regular, adherent, non-tender, and immobile; fluid thrill present on percussion; bowel sounds present
- **Cardiovascular exam:** normal heart sounds, no murmurs
- **Respiratory exam:** dull note on percussion with decreased air entry on the right side, suggesting a right-sided pleural effusion
- **Neurological exam:** no focal deficits
- **Coagulation profile:** PT 15 sec, INR 1.1, aPTT 30 sec — essentially normal
- **Ascitic fluid analysis:** high SAAG (1.5), low protein, consistent with a portal-hypertensive cause; total cell count 21 with a lymphocyte-predominant differential, RBCs present
- **Pleural fluid analysis:** transudative by Light's criteria, similar composition to the ascitic fluid (low protein, similar cell counts), raising suspicion for hepatic hydrothorax
- **Chest X-ray:** findings consistent with right pleural effusion
- **Triple-phase contrast CT and MR venogram:** a shrunken right lobe of the liver with hypertrophy of the left lobe, gross ascites, a large right pleural effusion with pleural thickening and collapse of the entire right lung, and multiple lesions in the vertebral bodies and ribs. There was severe narrowing of the intrahepatic portion of the inferior vena cava, with faint contrast filling at its cranial-most aspect — a picture suggestive of chronic Budd-Chiari syndrome. Sarcoidosis and metastatic disease were also raised as possibilities given the bone lesions.
- **Bone biopsy** (CT-guided, from the posterior iliac crest) was performed to evaluate the multiple hyperdense bone lesions seen on imaging.
- **Serology:** negative

sections.heading: How the Story Unfolded
sections.content:
Over the following weeks, the team grappled with an unusual combination: portal hypertension without deranged coagulation, ascites and a transudative pleural effusion that behaved as a single connected fluid compartment, and multiple sclerotic-appearing bone lesions whose cause remained unclear even after biopsy. Imaging pointed toward a vascular problem in the liver — narrowing of the intrahepatic inferior vena cava consistent with Budd-Chiari syndrome — but the additional bone involvement raised the question of a systemic infiltrative process such as sarcoidosis or metastatic disease underlying both the vascular obstruction and the skeletal findings, rather than a straightforward vascular event on its own.

She also developed restricted movement in her left shoulder, present for four months, which was referred to orthopedics; an X-ray of the shoulder showed only degenerative changes.

Despite ongoing management, the underlying cause of her portal hypertension, refractory ascites, and bone lesions was never definitively established during her hospital course. She passed away at home on 14 March 2021, with the cause of death uncertain.
